title: Bills of Exchange
tagline: Parties, terms and maturity of a bill, and the entries in the books of the drawer, drawee and endorsee.

overview.intro: Credit sales create a risk: the seller has parted with goods and holds only a promise to be paid. A bill of exchange turns that promise into a formal, negotiable instrument that can be presented at a fixed date, stamped as evidence, and even sold to a bank for cash before it matures. This unit covers the meaning and parties of a bill, the related instruments of promissory note and cheque, the calculation of term and maturity date, the journal and ledger entries in the books of the drawer and the drawee, endorsement, discounting, and what happens on acceptance and on dishonour. The entries are mechanical once the roles are fixed in the mind.

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: An unconditional written order by one party directing another to pay a certain sum on a specified date to or to the order of a third party.

facts.label: Parties
facts.value: Drawer who draws the bill, drawee who is ordered to pay and who accepts, payee who receives the money.

facts.label: Term
facts.value: Days after sight if the bill is presented for acceptance, otherwise days after date of issue.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Entries in the drawer’s books and the maturity-date calculation are regular numerical questions.

learningOutcomes: Define a bill of exchange and identify its three parties.
Distinguish a bill of exchange, a promissory note and a cheque.
Calculate the term and the maturity date of a bill including days of grace.
Pass journal entries in the books of the drawer and the drawee.
Explain endorsement, discounting and dishonour with their entries.

blocks.text: A bill of exchange is an unconditional written order, signed by the drawer, requiring the drawee to pay a certain and fixed amount of money on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time to a specified person or to that person’s order. Three parties are involved. The drawer draws the bill and is the party to whom money is owed. The drawee is ordered to pay and, by writing Accepted across the bill and signing it, becomes the primary debtor. The payee is the party entitled to receive payment, who may be the drawer itself or a person to whom the bill is endorsed.

blocks.caption: Essential parties and terms of a bill of exchange
rows: The person who makes the order to pay, usually the seller of goods
The person ordered to pay; on acceptance he becomes the acceptor
The person entitled to receive the money, often the drawer
The drawee’s signed promise on the face of the bill to honour it
The period of the bill, either after date or after sight
The date on which payment falls due, including days of grace
Transfer of the right to receive payment by signing the bill over to another party

items.text: Ravi sells goods to Sunil and draws a bill for ₹40,000 payable after 60 days.
items.note: Ravi is the drawer and payee, Sunil is the drawee who must accept, and the bill becomes due 60 days after the stated date.

items.text: Sunil accepts the bill and later endorses it to his own creditor Meera.
items.note: Sunil becomes the acceptor and Meera becomes the payee, so payment must be made to Meera on the maturity date.

learn.title: Bill, promissory note and cheque compared

blocks.text: Three instruments are often confused. A bill of exchange is an order to pay made by the creditor. A promissory note is an unconditional promise to pay made by the debtor himself, so there are only two parties: the maker who promises and the payee to whom the promise is made. A cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a bank and payable on demand, always payable immediately and never at a future date. The distinction matters in entries because the wording of the instrument determines who is promising and who is ordering.

blocks.caption: Comparison of bill of exchange, promissory note and cheque
rows: On a future date or on demand
Returned by the bank with a memo

items: A bill must be accepted before the drawee is primarily liable.
A promissory note needs no acceptance because the maker has already promised.
A cheque can be crossed to force collection through a bank.
All three are negotiable, meaning they can be transferred by endorsement and delivery.

learn.title: Term of the bill and the maturity date

blocks.text: The term of a bill is stated either as days after date, counted from the date on which the bill was drawn, or as days after sight, counted from the date on which the drawee first saw and accepted it. When the term is given in months, the maturity date falls on the corresponding date of the due month: a bill dated 15 January for three months matures on 15 April. Three days of grace are added by law to every term bill, so a bill drawn on 1 March for 60 days after date falls due on 30 April once the term is counted, and becomes legally payable on 3 May after the three days of grace are added.

blocks.caption: Working out the maturity date
rows: Date of issue for days after date, date of acceptance for days after sight
Count the exact number of days or months from the starting point
Every term bill gains three legal days of grace
If a month has no corresponding date, take the last day of that month

items.text: Bill dated 10 February for 30 days after date.
items.note: Thirty days from 10 February is 12 March, and three days of grace make the maturity date 15 March.

items.text: Bill dated 31 January for one month.
items.note: There is no 31 February, so the month ends on 28 February and with three days of grace the bill is due on 3 March.

learn.title: Entries in the books of the drawer and the drawee

blocks.text: When the drawer receives a bill from the drawee, no entry is passed in the drawer’s books for mere acceptance, because acceptance does not change the debt; the bill receivable is a memorandum only until it is honoured or dishonoured. When the bill is discharged, the drawer debits bank and credits bills receivable, and the drawee debits bills payable and credits bank. On dishonour, the drawer reverses the original position by debiting the drawee’s account and crediting bills receivable, restoring the open account exactly as it stood before the bill was drawn.

blocks.caption: Journal entries for a bill of exchange
rows: Bills payable account opened by acceptance
Drawer’s personal a/c Dr, to Bills receivable
Bills payable Dr, to Drawer’s personal a/c
Bill renewed with a new bill and interest
Interest a/c Dr, to Drawer (new bill drawn later)

blocks.text: When a bill is dishonoured and the drawee cannot pay, a new bill is often drawn for the amount plus interest for the extended credit. The interest is an expense of the drawee and an income of the drawer, and it must be recorded before the new bill is drawn. If the drawee becomes insolvent, only the amount actually received under a final dividend is recorded and the balance is a bad debt.

items.text: Drawer receives a bill for ₹25,000, dishonoured and then renewed with ₹500 interest.
items.note: On dishonour: Sunil Dr 25,000 to Bills receivable 25,000. For renewal: Interest Dr 500 to Sunil 500, then a new bill of ₹25,500 is accepted.

items.text: Bill discounted with a bank for ₹19,400 when its face value is ₹20,000.
items.note: Bank Dr 19,400, Discount allowed Dr 600, to Bills receivable 20,000.

blocks.text: A payee who owes money elsewhere can transfer the bill instead of waiting for maturity. Endorsement means signing the bill on the back and delivering it to another party, who then becomes the payee and can enforce payment. Discounting means selling the bill to a bank before its due date; the bank pays the face value less a discount charge for the period remaining. Both routes end the drawer’s risk only if the bill is honoured; if it is dishonoured, the bank or endorsee returns it and the original party must pay, which is why an endorsement carries the hidden liability of a contingent debt.

items: Endorsement transfers the right to receive payment by signature and delivery.
A bill may be endorsed more than once, forming an endorsement chain.
Discounting converts a future receipt into present cash at a cost.
A bill can be sent to the bank for collection, where the bank only collects and does not advance money.
Surety or guarantee is a separate contract by a third party to pay if the acceptor defaults.

blocks.caption: Options available to the holder of a bill
rows: Collect the face value on the due date
Bank pays face value less discount
Bank collects on maturity and remits

figures.description: Three boxes in a triangle: drawer on the left issuing an arrow labelled drawn bill to the drawee at the top, the drawee returning an accepted bill, and a final arrow from the drawee to the payee on the right marked payment at maturity.
labels: Drawer: the seller who orders the payment
Drawee: the buyer who accepts and becomes the acceptor
Payee: the party entitled to receive the money
Acceptance is signed across the face of the bill
Payment is made to the payee on the maturity date

figures.caption: Figure: The life of a bill from drawing to discharge
figures.description: A horizontal timeline with five milestones: drawn, accepted, discounted or endorsed, presented for payment, and finally discharged or dishonoured with a branch leading to renewal with interest.
labels: Drawn: the drawer issues the bill for goods supplied
Accepted: the drawee signs and becomes primarily liable
Transferred: endorsed to another party or discounted with a bank
Maturity: term plus three days of grace
Discharged when paid, or dishonoured and renewed with interest

keyPoints: A bill of exchange is an unconditional written order to pay a certain sum on a fixed future date.
The three parties are the drawer, the drawee and the payee; on acceptance the drawee becomes the acceptor.
A promissory note is a promise, not an order, and has only two parties.
A cheque is a bill drawn on a bank and payable always on demand.
The term runs after date or after sight, and three days of grace are added to find the maturity date.
No entry is passed in the drawer’s books when a bill is merely accepted.
On dishonour the drawer’s personal account is debited and bills receivable credited.
Renewal requires interest, recorded as an expense of the acceptor and income of the drawer.
Discounting a bill gives cash before maturity at the cost of the discount charged by the bank.
Endorsement transfers the right to payment but leaves a contingent liability if the bill is dishonoured.
examFocus: Maturity-date questions are answered in three steps: starting point, term, three days of grace; show all three in the working.
State the position for each party separately in narrative questions, because marks are given for the drawer, the drawee and the payee in turn.
In dishonour and renewal questions, record interest before drawing the new bill; marking the interest afterwards loses marks.

vocabulary.meaning: Unconditional written order to pay a fixed sum on a future date to a named person or order.
Party who draws the bill and is usually the seller owed the money.
The drawee after signing acceptance on the bill; the primary debtor.
Date on which a bill falls due after adding the term and three days of grace.
Transfer of a bill to another party by signing it on the back and delivering it.
Selling a bill to a bank before maturity for the face value less a charge.
Three extra days allowed by law before a term bill becomes legally due.

options: An order to pay made by the creditor
A promise to pay made by the debtor
An order drawn only on a bank
A receipt given by the seller
questions.answer: An order to pay made by the creditor
questions.explanation: The drawer orders the drawee to pay; a promise would be a promissory note and an order on a bank is a cheque.

questions.prompt: When a bill is accepted, in the drawer’s books:
options: Bank is debited and bills receivable credited
No entry is passed until the bill is honoured or dishonoured
Bills receivable is debited and the drawee credited
questions.answer: No entry is passed until the bill is honoured or dishonoured
questions.explanation: Acceptance does not itself settle the debt or create a receipt, so the drawer records the bill only as a memorandum until maturity.

questions.prompt: A bill drawn on 10 February for 30 days after date matures on:
questions.explanation: Thirty days from 10 February reaches 12 March, and three days of grace take the maturity date to 15 March.

questions.prompt: On dishonour of a bill of ₹18,000, the entry in the drawer’s books is:
questions.explanation: The bill is cancelled and the drawee’s open account is restored by debiting the drawee and crediting bills receivable.

questions.prompt: The person who draws a bill of exchange and orders the payment is called the __________ .
questions.explanation: The drawer issues the order and is usually the seller who is owed the money for goods supplied.

questions.prompt: Three additional days allowed by law before a term bill becomes legally due are called days of __________ .
questions.explanation: Grace days are added to the term to give the parties time to complete formalities, and they apply to every term bill.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a bill of exchange from a promissory note on three points.
questions.answer: First, a bill is an order to pay while a promissory note is a promise to pay. Second, a bill has three parties, drawer, drawee and payee, while a note has only two, the maker and the payee. Third, a bill requires the drawee’s acceptance before he becomes primarily liable, whereas a note needs no acceptance because the maker has already committed himself.
questions.explanation: Three contrasts are needed for full marks; two earn partial credit.

questions.prompt: What is meant by discounting a bill, and what entry does the drawer pass?
questions.answer: Discounting means selling a bill to a bank before its maturity date; the bank pays the face value less a discount charged for the unexpired period. The drawer debits Bank with the amount received, debits Discount Allowed with the charge, and credits Bills Receivable with the face value of the bill.
questions.explanation: Both the meaning and the three-part entry are required; the discount allowed debit is the element most often omitted.

questions.prompt: Ravi draws a bill on Sunil for ₹30,000 which is dishonoured and then renewed with interest of ₹600. Give the entries in the books of both parties.
questions.answer: In Ravi’s books, on dishonour: Sunil Dr 30,000 to Bills receivable 30,000. For interest: Interest Dr 600 to Sunil 600. When the new bill for ₹30,600 is accepted, it is recorded as a memorandum. In Sunil’s books, on dishonour: Bills payable Dr 30,000 to Ravi 30,000; for interest: Ravi Dr 600 to Interest 600; the new bill of ₹30,600 is then accepted.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the reversal in both books and the interest recorded before the renewal, because interest is the income of one party and the expense of the other.

questions.prompt: A bill for ₹24,000 is dishonoured and the acceptor pays ₹15,000 in cash immediately and agrees to give a new bill for the balance plus ₹400 interest. Pass the entries in the drawer’s books.
questions.answer: On dishonour: Acceptor Dr 24,000 to Bills receivable 24,000. On receiving cash: Bank or Cash Dr 15,000 to Acceptor 15,000. For interest: Interest Dr 400 to Acceptor 400, making the amount due ₹9,400. When the new bill for ₹9,400 is drawn and accepted, no entry is made in the drawer’s books until maturity, the bill being kept as a memorandum of the amount now outstanding.
questions.explanation: The sequence tests whether the student keeps the personal account as the running balance: cash reduces it, interest increases it, and only the new bill settles the residual.
